bp: A search engine is supposed to be a way of sampling the web for independent evidence. A person asks a question, the system sorts a huge pile of pages, and the top results become the facts that downstream tools and readers see. This paper asks what happens when a growing share of that pile is not original human evidence but AI-written text, especially text produced by large language models, systems that generate fluent answers from learned text patterns. The risk is not just that some pages are bad. The deeper risk is circular: web search retrieves AI-written pages, retrieval-augmented generation systems use those pages as evidence, and new AI-written pages then echo the same material back into the web. The paper calls this Retrieval Collapse: first, synthetic sources take over exposure and reduce source diversity; then low-quality or adversarial sources enter the retrieval pipeline.
wh: The hard part is that failure can look like success from the outside. Ordinary spam often has visible clues: strange wording, irrelevant keywords, or obvious manipulation. High-quality SEO-style AI content can instead be fluent, topical, and good enough to preserve answer accuracy in the short term. That creates a deceptively healthy state: the answer may still be right, while the evidence base has quietly narrowed to recycled synthetic sources. The abstract reports exactly this kind of mismatch: when the candidate pool was 67% contaminated, exposure contamination rose above 80%, yet answer accuracy remained stable. A second difficulty is adversarial contamination. A bad actor can craft content that seems relevant to the search system while carrying harmful or manipulative instructions. Retrieval systems therefore face two tensions at once: preserving diverse original sources and suppressing dangerous sources without simply rejecting every AI-looking page.
naive: A smart beginner might say: just rank pages by relevance, then check whether the final answer is accurate. If the answer remains correct, the system is fine. This fails because relevance and provenance are different questions. A synthetic page can match the query and repeat a true claim while still replacing independent evidence with recycled text. Accuracy also misses delayed damage: once synthetic pages dominate exposure, future systems train on and retrieve from a thinner, less diverse web. Another beginner fix is to use a standard keyword ranker such as BM25, which scores documents by matching query words against document words. But keyword matching cannot reliably tell helpful synthetic text from adversarial synthetic text.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat retrieval pollution as an ecosystem process, not as a one-document quality problem. It separates the collapse into two stages. In the first stage, AI-generated content becomes common enough in the searchable pool that the top results are disproportionately synthetic, reducing the variety of sources users and RAG systems see. In the second stage, low-quality or adversarial content enters the same pipeline and can influence the evidence shown to a model or user. The experiments make these stages visible by controlling the kind and amount of contamination. One setting uses high-quality SEO-style synthetic content, the kind that can look useful and harmless. Another uses adversarially crafted content, where the question is whether rankers can keep harmful material out. The comparison includes BM25 and LLM-based rankers, which use a language model to judge or reorder candidates.
mech: The mechanism starts with a retrieval pool: a set of candidate web pages or page-like documents that a search system could return for a query. The experiment changes the makeup of that pool by adding controlled amounts of AI-generated material. In the SEO-style setting, the synthetic material is designed to be relevant and polished, so the test is not merely whether the search engine can spot junk. The system then ranks candidates and exposes a small top portion to users or to a RAG pipeline. The key measurement is not only pool contamination, meaning the share of synthetic material available, but exposure contamination, meaning the share of synthetic material that actually appears in the results people or models consume. The abstract reports a sharp amplification: 67% contamination in the pool produced more than 80% contamination in exposure. The paper also keeps track of answer accuracy, showing that surface correctness can remain stable even when evidence diversity erodes. In the adversarial setting, the input includes harmful crafted content. Different rankers then score or reorder the candidates. BM25, a word-overlap scoring rule, exposed about 19% harmful content, while LLM-based rankers suppressed it more strongly.
math: The main mathematics is ranking under contamination. Ranking means turning many candidate documents into an ordered list by assigning each candidate a score for the current query. BM25 is a classic scoring rule: it counts useful word matches while correcting for words that are common everywhere and for document length. This is a good first language for search because many information needs are partly expressed by shared words, but it is blind to source origin and intent unless those facts affect the words. The paper also uses the mathematics of proportions and exposure. Pool contamination is a fraction of the available evidence; exposure contamination is a fraction of what the ranking system actually shows. Comparing those two fractions reveals amplification: the ranking process can make a polluted pool look even more polluted at the top. In adversarial tests, the mathematical object is a decision boundary: harmful versus acceptable content after scoring. LLM-based rankers add a richer scoring function, where a language model evaluates meaning and likely harm rather than only word overlap. The tradeoff is speed and simplicity versus deeper judgment, and relevance versus source diversity.
dots: This paper connects directly to the repository's Information Retrieval & Search family, where 465 papers are grouped around choosing useful evidence from huge collections, and to the Retrieval-Augmented RAG family, where 182 papers study systems that retrieve documents before generating answers. It is closest to the robustness branch: the family data includes Conflict-Aware RAG, OpenDecoder, poisoning and attack papers, and multimodal RAG security work. Those papers share a hidden problem with this one: retrieval is no longer just finding something relevant; it must decide which evidence deserves to enter an answer-making pipeline. The paper also links to ranking, because top positions define what evidence counts; to probability, because contamination rates estimate ecosystem risk from repeated trials; and to misinformation or trust, because synthetic content can be plausible without being independent. Its special contribution is to frame pollution as a self-reinforcing web-level cycle.
ww: The approach works because it measures the failure at the place where harm appears: the exposed evidence, not only the raw web pool or the final answer. If synthetic pages are 67% of the pool but more than 80% of the shown results, then ranking is not a neutral window into the web; it is concentrating the pollution. That observation would be invisible if one only checked answer accuracy. The split between SEO-style and adversarial content is also important. Polished synthetic content tests whether systems can preserve source diversity when badness is subtle. Adversarial content tests whether systems can keep deliberately harmful material out. Comparing BM25 with LLM-based rankers then explains why richer judgment can help: word overlap sees topical match, while a language model ranker can use broader cues about meaning and harmful intent. The result is not that language model rankers solve collapse. It is that different failure modes require different defenses: provenance and diversity controls for quiet homogenization, stronger semantic screening for adversarial infiltration.
po: The payoff is a clearer warning signal for web-grounded systems. The paper shows that a retrieval pipeline can become heavily dependent on synthetic evidence while ordinary answer accuracy still looks stable. It also quantifies two concrete risks from the abstract: more than 80% exposure contamination under a 67% contaminated SEO-style pool, and about 19% harmful exposure for BM25 under adversarial contamination. LLM-based rankers suppress adversarial content more strongly, suggesting that ranker design matters. The practical capability is diagnostic: builders can evaluate whether their retrieval stack is preserving source diversity and resisting harmful infiltration, instead of only asking whether answers look correct today.
limits: The abstract supports strong claims about controlled experiments, not a complete measurement of the entire live web. The results depend on how the SEO-style and adversarial content were created, which queries were used, which rankers were tested, and how exposure and harm were labeled. Stable answer accuracy in the experiment does not prove long-term safety; it is part of the warning, because short-term correctness can hide source collapse. LLM-based rankers suppress adversarial content better in the reported setting, but the abstract does not prove they will catch adaptive attacks or preserve diversity. The paper also assumes that synthetic provenance and source diversity are important for trustworthy retrieval, an assumption that is plausible but still needs system-specific policy choices.
